q: Explain why one primary oocyte gives only one egg.
In both divisions of meiosis the cytoplasm divides unequally: the polar bodies get very little and break down, so the egg keeps the food reserves.
Calculate the number of eggs a woman releases in her life with no pregnancies, at one per 28-day cycle.
365 / 28 = 13 per year; 13 × 35 = about 455 eggs.
Calculate the percentage of the oocytes present at puberty that are ever released.
Suggest why males make so many more gametes than females.
Sperm are small and cheap to make, and almost all of them fail to reach the egg; the egg is large and costly because it supports the early embryo.
Compare the sizes of the two gametes and explain the difference.
The egg is 24 times wider (thousands of times the volume). It holds cytoplasm, nutrients and organelles for the embryo; the sperm is streamlined for swimming.

16.t: Working with data: hCG in early pregnancy
q: A home test detects 25 IU per litre. Estimate the day it would first be positive in the healthy pregnancy.
Between day 7 and day 10 (about day 9).
Calculate how many times hCG increases from day 14 to day 28 in the healthy pregnancy.
Explain why hCG is needed in early pregnancy.
hCG keeps the corpus luteum secreting progesterone, which maintains the endometrium and prevents menstruation.
In a healthy pregnancy hCG roughly doubles every 2 to 3 days. Evaluate whether patient Z’s pregnancy is developing normally.

Z’s hCG rises but too slowly: from day 14 to 21 it does not even double three times (90 to 210, against 250 to 2500). This suggests a problem such as a failing or ectopic pregnancy, but one set of values is not enough: a scan is needed.
Suggest why a test on day 7 can be negative even in a healthy pregnancy.
Implantation happens around days 6 to 10, so little hCG has been made yet; the level (5) is below the test’s limit.

23.t: Working with data: two kinds of study
q: Calculate the percentage difference in CHD for HRT users compared with non-users in each study.
Observational: (30 − 45) / 45 = 33% lower. Trial: (37 − 30) / 30 = 23% higher.
Explain why the observational study suggested that HRT protects the heart.
Women chose whether to take HRT, and those who did were healthier (wealthier, more exercise): confounding variables, not HRT, lowered their CHD.
Explain why the randomised trial is more reliable.
Random allocation spreads other factors evenly between the groups, and a placebo keeps the trial blind, so the only systematic difference is HRT.
The trial was stopped early. Suggest why.
It showed harm (more CHD and other disease in the HRT group), so it was unethical to continue.
The observational study had four times as many women. Explain why its conclusion was still less reliable.
A large sample reduces random error, but it does not remove bias from confounding variables.
